# Education in Nigeria
Nigeria’s education system begins with primary education starting around age 5, lasting six years, culminating with a first school-leaving certificate. The curriculum includes core subjects such as Mathematics, English, religious knowledge (Christian and Islamic), agricultural science, home economics, and indigenous languages (Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba, Igbo), with private schools often adding Computer Science, French, and Fine Arts. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) program mandates nine years of free and compulsory schooling covering six years of primary and three years of junior secondary school, monitored by the Universal Basic Education Commission. Transition to secondary education follows the "6-3-3-4" system, with three years each in Junior and Senior Secondary School. Senior Secondary curriculum includes core and elective subjects spanning sciences, humanities, and vocational topics. Federal, state, and private secondary schools vary in funding, quality, and teacher qualifications, with federal schools generally offering better resources and merit-based admissions.
Tertiary education consists of universities (federal, state, private), polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education. Admission requires relevant secondary certificates and satisfactory scores in standardized entrance exams. Vocational education is overseen by the National Board for Technical Education, offering certificates such as National Technical Certificate and Advanced National Technical Certificate, supplemented by apprenticeships. Despite efforts, challenges persist due to teacher shortages, inadequate funding, and infrastructure gaps, especially in rural areas. Literacy rates remain low overall (~62% adult literacy in 2018), with regional disparities worsened by poverty and insecurity. Female education faces barriers including cultural factors and insecurity, though initiatives like UNICEF’s Girls’ Education Project aim to improve enrollment and retention. Informal education, including literacy programs and apprenticeships, plays a significant role but suffers from lack of coordination and funding. International schools and advanced level programs (IJMB, JUPEB) provide alternative pathways aligned with international standards. The government continues efforts to improve literacy and educational quality, including digital literacy targets and policy reforms.
